title: Possession with Apostrophes and Of
summary: Use an apostrophe to connect people with things and relationships. Distinguish singular and plural possessive forms, omit a repeated noun when it is clear, and use of in common expressions about things and places.
learningObjectives: Form the possessive of a singular person with apostrophe s.
Write plural possessives correctly, including irregular plurals such as children.
Use a possessive form without a repeated noun when the meaning is clear.
Choose natural expressions with of for parts of things and locations.

explanation.heading: Show a connection to one person with 's
explanation.body: Add apostrophe s ('s) to a singular name or noun to show ownership or a relationship: a person's coat, a friend's sister, or a teacher's desk. This form usually comes directly before the noun. Some names already end in s; a form such as James's is common.
explanation.example: Aisha's brother works in a bakery.

explanation.heading: Plural possessives have two patterns
explanation.body: If a plural already ends in s, add only an apostrophe: the students' bags or my neighbours' garden. If a plural does not end in s, add apostrophe s: the children's coats or the men's room. Check whether the owner is one person or several.

explanation.heading: The noun can be left out when it is understood
explanation.body: You do not always need to repeat the noun after a possessive. If the context names two coats, hers may be different from her sister's, meaning her sister's coat. We also use a person's possessive form alone to mean their home in expressions such as at Rosa's.
explanation.example: We had coffee at Mateo's on Sunday.

explanation.heading: Use of in many expressions about things and places
explanation.body: For parts of objects, positions and place names, English often uses of: the front of the bus, the end of the road, or the centre of the town. Do not assume that every noun takes an apostrophe; learn common of expressions as complete phrases.
explanation.example: The handle of this suitcase is broken.

comparisons.title: One owner or more than one owner

left.label: One friend
left.note: Friend's describes one friend who owns the bicycle.

right.label: Several friends
right.note: Friends' refers to two or more friends.

left.label: A person
left.example: Nadia's phone is on the shelf.
left.note: Apostrophe s is the ordinary form for a person's possession.

right.label: Part of an object
right.example: The screen of the phone is cracked.
right.note: Of is a natural choice for identifying a part of a thing.

examples.note: Cousin's identifies one person connected with the raincoat.

examples.sentence: The workers' bicycles are behind the office.
examples.note: Workers' is plural because the bicycles belong to several workers.

examples.sentence: Mila's bag is smaller than Theo's.
examples.note: Theo's stands for Theo's bag, so bag does not need to be repeated.

examples.sentence: There is a café at the end of the street.
examples.note: The end of the street is a common expression with of.

commonMistakes.why: Add apostrophe s to Maria to express possession.
The regular plural parents already ends in s, so add only an apostrophe.
Children is an irregular plural without final s, so use children's.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I spent the afternoon at Noah house.
commonMistakes.correct: I spent the afternoon at Noah's house.
commonMistakes.why: Use Noah's before house to identify whose house it is.

studyTips: First decide how many owners there are: one teacher's desk, two teachers' desks, or the children's desks.
For familiar people, practise using 's with names and family words: Ben's cousin, my aunt's shop and our parents' garden.
Learn common phrases with of, such as the middle of the page and the top of the hill, as whole expressions.

exercises.prompt: One student owns this laptop. It's the ___ laptop.
exercises.feedback: Student's is singular because only one student owns the laptop.

exercises.prompt: The twins share a bedroom. It is the ___ bedroom.
exercises.feedback: Twins is a plural ending in s, so the possessive is twins'.

exercises.prompt: These toys belong to the children. They are the ___ toys.
exercises.feedback: Children is an irregular plural without final s, so the possessive is children's.

exercises.prompt: We stayed at ___ last night. (Lara invited us to her home.)
exercises.feedback: At Lara's can mean at Lara's home without repeating the word home.

exercises.prompt: My uncle has a dog. This is my ___ dog.
exercises.feedback: Uncle's is the possessive form for one uncle.

exercises.prompt: My two neighbours share a garden. It's my ___ garden. (Both neighbours own it.)
exercises.feedback: Neighbours' ends in an apostrophe because the garden belongs to both neighbours.

exercises.prompt: The boys have one football between them. It's the ___ football.
exercises.feedback: Boys' shows shared possession by more than one boy.

exercises.prompt: The cover ___ this magazine has a photograph of a mountain.
exercises.feedback: The cover of this magazine identifies a part of an object, using of.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I borrowed my sisters coat. (I have one sister.)
exercises.feedback: With one sister, put apostrophe s after sister.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: These are my parents's suitcases.
exercises.feedback: For regular plural parents, write the apostrophe after the final s.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: The childrens' playground is behind the school.
acceptedAnswers: The children's playground is behind the school.
exercises.feedback: The irregular plural children needs apostrophe s, not s apostrophe.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: We ate lunch at Dylan house.
acceptedAnswers: We ate lunch at Dylan's house.
exercises.feedback: Use Dylan's before house to express a person's possession.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say this camera belongs to Hannah. Start with 'This is' and use the possessive form.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hannah's identifies the person who owns the camera.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that the bicycles belong to your two brothers. Start with 'These are'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Brothers' is the possessive for two brothers.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say you spent last Saturday evening at Nora's house, without saying 'house'. Start with 'I was'.
acceptedAnswers: I was at Nora's last Saturday evening.
speakingExercises.feedback: At Nora's uses a person's possessive form to mean at Nora's home.

speakingExercises.prompt: Mr Lee has a daughter who works in his shop. Tell a visitor who she is, beginning with 'She is' and using a possessive name.
speakingExercises.feedback: Add apostrophe s to Mr Lee to describe his family relationship: Mr Lee's daughter.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change 'The child's coats are wet' so that the coats belong to several children. Say the whole sentence.
speakingExercises.feedback: Children is an irregular plural, so its possessive form is children's; this is different from child's.

speakingExercises.prompt: Three men share a van for work. Someone asks, 'Whose van is parked outside?' Reply using 'men's', beginning with 'It's'.
speakingExercises.feedback: Men is an irregular plural, so the possessive is men's, not mens'.

speakingExercises.prompt: Express 'The bicycle's front wheel is bent' with an 'of' phrase instead of apostrophe s. Start with 'The front wheel'.
acceptedAnswers: The front wheel of the bicycle is bent.
speakingExercises.feedback: For a part of an object, the front wheel of the bicycle is a natural expression.

speakingExercises.prompt: Sara's coat is black, and Ben's coat is blue. Combine the facts in one sentence beginning 'Sara's coat' and do not repeat the word 'coat'.
acceptedAnswers: Sara's coat is black, but Ben's is blue.
Sara's coat is black, and Ben's is blue.
speakingExercises.feedback: Ben's can stand alone because the noun coat is already understood.

listeningExercises.audioText: My friends' flat is close to the park, and they share the rent.
listeningExercises.prompt: How many friends does the speaker mean?
listeningExercises.feedback: Friends' refers to more than one friend who share the flat.

listeningExercises.audioText: We met at Clara's after the concert and made some tea.
listeningExercises.feedback: At Clara's means at Clara's home; the meeting happened after the concert.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children's shoes are under the bench.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the possessive word that comes immediately before 'shoes'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Children's is the possessive form of the irregular plural children.

listeningExercises.audioText: My brother's keys are in the drawer, but Mum's are next to the kettle.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who owns the keys near the kettle?
listeningExercises.feedback: Mum's means Mum's keys; the brother's keys are in a different place.

listeningExercises.audioText: The children's coach waited outside the gym, but the parents' cars were in the car park.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which vehicles were in the car park?
listeningExercises.feedback: The audio says the parents' cars were in the car park; the coach waited outside the gym.

listeningExercises.audioText: The handle of the suitcase came off, so Lena took it to the repair shop.
choices: The part used to carry the suitcase.
listeningExercises.feedback: The handle of the suitcase is the part used to carry it; of identifies a part of an object.

listeningExercises.audioText: The women's changing room is on the first floor, near the stairs.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the possessive word you hear immediately before 'changing room'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Women's is the possessive form of the irregular plural women.

listeningExercises.audioText: The bottom of the swimming pool is painted bright blue.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the short word you hear between 'bottom' and 'the swimming pool'.
listeningExercises.feedback: Of connects the part, bottom, with the whole object, the swimming pool.
